newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico opposition weakens PRI power in congress.
newsitem.headline: Mexico opposition weakens PRI power in congress.

text.p: Mexican opposition parties have banded together to weaken the decades-long control of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) over legislation in the lower house of Congress.
The informal accord between Mexico's four major opposition parties on Monday does not aim to bridge their stark ideological differences to outvote the PRI on every bill.

But the agreement does seek to strip the PRI's historic control from every major congressional committee and loosen its grip over day-to-day business in the lower house for the first time in 68 years.

"After several weeks of discussions, the opposition has agreed on certain basic concepts of running the lower house," said Santiago Creel, a former electoral official who organised the opposition meeting at his Mexico City home.

In historic elections on July 6, advances by the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and conservative National Action Party (PAN) cost President Ernesto Zedillo's PRI its absolute majority in the Chamber of Deputies.

The PRD and PAN, together with Mexico's Green Party (PVEM) and the Workers' Party (PT), garnered a combined total of 261 votes in the 500 seat house, which convenes in September. The PRI won the remaining 239 seats.

Among other things, the parties agreed to block PRI control over a main congressional committee that sets the rules of procedure and is similar to the U.S. House of Representatives' Ways and Means Committee.
They also will appoint independent bureaucrats to oversee the chamber's internal finances and management.
Despite the show of unity from the agreement, analysts say the opposition is unlikely to stick together when it comes to the nuts and bolts of legislation.
The first crack in the opposition's united voice could come soon, when lawmakers vote on a controversial proposal to lower Mexico's value-added tax.
PRD congressional leader Porfirio Munoz Ledo last weekend said he wanted to cut the tax from 15 percent to 10 percent right away, while the PAN has favoured a go-slow approach.
"Any pretense of unity will be shattered on the first bill that comes up for a vote," said Jaime Gonzalez Graf, head of the Mexican Institute of Political Studies.
"But this agreement is an historic, revolutionary event. For the first time in decades, the PRI will not be able to dictate everything that happens in the lower house," he said.
